newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenian parliament to vote on PM on Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: Slovenian parliament to vote on PM on Wednesday.

text.p: Slovenia's parliament will vote on Wednesday on whether to back the candidacy of acting Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek to lead a new government, officials said on Monday.
"Leaders of the parliamentary party groups decided today the vote will be taken on Wednesday morning," Matjaz Kozelj of the parliamentary speaker's office told Reuters.
Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats emerged as the strongest single party in a general election on November 10, winning 25 out of 90 parliamentary seats.
But chances of Drnovsek, 46, returning to power in the former Yugoslav republic appeared increasingly slim.

Drnovsek, nominated by President Milan Kucan last week to seek support to form a new government, is pitted against an alliance of three rightwing parties, which together hold 45 seats -- just one short of an absolute majority.
Even if Drnovsek wins backing from all the other parliamentary parties, including former communists, he would also be short of one seat for an absolute majority.
The likelihood of him persuading one of the rightwing parties to break away from the so-called "Spring" alliance appeared increasingly remote.
The alliance, comprising the conservative People's Party, led by the youthful Marjan Podobnik, the centre-right Social Democrats and the Chistian Democrats, remained united.
"We expect that we will get the support in a second round (of voting)..and believe we will form the government," Podobnik said last week.
The rightwing parties are pressing for Podobnik, 36, to be the new prime minister heading a coalition which will push Slovenian politics sharply to the right.

"The way it looks now Drnovsek's chances are very small. The chance of Podobnik getting elected in the second round is greater," Igor Luksic, a professor of politics at Ljubljana University's Faculty of Social Sciences, told Reuters.
Podobnik's People's Party, which believes in Roman Catholic and family values, is strongly supported by Slovenia's farming lobby, suspicious of rash membership of the European Union.

Podobnik has already signalled that EU entry would have to provide guarantees to support farmers and other Slovenian national interests -- a position which is likely to delay membership beyond the estimated entry date of 2001.

Drnovsek, a former president of Yugoslavia and strong pro-European, on Monday signed a cooperation agreement with the small Desus party, a group representing pensioners with five seats in parliament, thus securing their votes on Wednesday.
He is scheduled to sign a similar agreement on Tuesday with the United List of Social Democrats, the former communists.
